entries.title: Do not feed the animals. Vets explain why hats, coins and shoes can be deadly.
entries.summary: It's not easy to retrieve foreign objects from animals once ingested. Some things can be grabbed using an endoscope. But if an item gets far into the intestinal tract, surgery isn't always possible.
entries.content:
Do not feed the animals. Vets explain why hats, coins and shoes can be deadly.

The death of Fiona, a beloved hippopotamus who captured hearts, has renewed calls to remind zoo visitors that animals can die from swallowing foreign objects.

Fiona, 9 years old, died Thursday after ingesting a hat that accidentally ended up in her habitat at the Cincinnati Zoo. The zoo said that the hat was lodged in the hippo's small intestine and surgery was not possible.

"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Cincinnati Zoo Director Dave Jenike said in a statement.

While deaths are rare, items such as coins, shoes and sunglasses frequently fall, and sometimes are tossed, into animal enclosures.

In 2024, 70 U.S. coins were successfully removed from an alligator at Omaha's Henry Doorly Zoo and Aquarium. And in 2025, a Komodo dragon ate a shoe that was thrown into its habitat at the Memphis Zoo. The shoe was removed and the dragon survived.

Dr. Gabriella Flacke, an associate veterinarian at Zoo Miami, said the zoo's staff have retrieved items such as cellphones from alligators.

"We've had to remove those items both endoscopically, which is basically putting a camera through the mouth and down into the stomach to grab and retrieve those items, or we've in a few cases had to do surgery where they were larger items that couldn't be removed that way," Flacke told NPR.

Recovering items from an alligator is easier than a hippo, she said. Unlike the alligator, which has a digestive system with one stomach divided into two parts, hippos have a multichambered stomach. This can make retrieving objects, such as the small hat that Fiona ingested, difficult, according to Dr. Jen Quammen, president of the American Veterinary Medical Association.

"It's not necessarily always the shape or size of the object, but it's maybe the twists and turns, metaphorically and physiologically, that things have to go through," Quammen told NPR.

Be aware that the animals have specialized dietary needs and requirements that caretakers provide them, Flacke said. She also asked visitors to follow zoo etiquette and not yell or throw objects at the animals.

"Anything that we bring that could inadvertently end up in the animal exhibit or somehow around the animal, try to just be mindful and not have your sunglasses on your head if you're leaning over and looking at something," she said. "If your child has a toy in its hand and you're walking around, it could just decide to throw the toy, whether it's thinking about that or not."

It's not just dangerous for zoo animals

Both Quammen and Flacke said people should not only be mindful of items that can harm animals at the zoo, but also what could hurt animals in the wild or pets at home.

Animals explore the world by putting things in their mouths, making them naturally curious about items that can be dangerous, Quammen said.

To help prevent an animal from ingesting something dangerous, one should dispose of their trash and properly store items such as human medicines in a place where an animal cannot reach it.

"Don't feed an animal without permission and that includes our pets at home, but also wildlife," added Quammen.

entries.title: What it's like at a climate conference as talks collapse
entries.summary: After two weeks of negotiations, international climate talks fail to reach an agreement. NPR's Rachel Waldholz was in Turkey for the conference.
entries.content:
What it's like at a climate conference as talks collapse

What it's like in the halls of a climate conference as it collapses

After two weeks of negotiations, international climate talks fail to reach an agreement. NPR's Rachel Waldholz was in Turkey for the conference.

ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:

International climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, ended today after negotiations fell apart. NPR's Rachel Waldholz has been at the conference and sent us this report.

RACHEL WALDHOLZ, BYLINE: I'm here in the Antalya Expo Center, which, for the past two weeks, has been packed with some 70,000 people who came to the COP31 climate conference. Now it's almost completely empty. In fact, they're disassembling parts of the venue around me. The climate talks ran two days past their scheduled end. By the time the gavel fell, many negotiators had already left to catch their flights home. Australia climate chief Chris Bowen led the negotiations.

CHRIS BOWEN: I haven't slept for the last three nights, been negotiating all the way through, but more importantly, people on delegations came at it and gave it everything they had.

WALDHOLZ: Delegates came to Antalya with long wish lists, from electrifying more of the global economy to money for developing countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change. Looming over it all is that this is the first summit to squarely face the reality that the planet will miss a key target of the Paris Climate Agreement, reaching warming of 1.5 degrees Celsius or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit above pre-Industrial levels. The U.N. says limiting that overshoot requires cutting the use of fossil fuels nearly in half in the next 10 to 15 years. Many countries wanted an agreement explicitly calling for a transition away from coal, oil and natural gas. But big oil-producing countries, like Saudi Arabia, blocked any mention of fossil fuels. Ultimately, the European Union decided no deal was better than the deal on the table. Darragh O'Brien is Ireland's environment minister.

DARRAGH O'BRIEN: We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.

WALDHOLZ: Many negotiators left the expo center dragging their suitcases on the way to the airport. They'll pick up negotiations next year at the next climate summit in Ethiopia. I'm Rachel Waldholz in Antalya, Turkey.

(SOUNDBITE OF SOFTLY'S "FLORA")

entries.title: Philly festival-goers say pickles are a real big dill
entries.summary: Influencer and pickle enthusiast Dan Pancoast gives a first hand account of the festivities at the "The Big Dill" festival in Philadelphia.
entries.content:
Philly festival-goers say pickles are a real big dill

Love 'em or hate 'em, folks at a festival in Philly say pickles are a real big dill

Influencer and pickle enthusiast Dan Pancoast gives a first hand account of the festivities at the "The Big Dill" festival in Philadelphia.

ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:

We are now going to turn to pickles, a food that has seemed to follow me my whole life. When I was growing up, I used to watch my mom and grandma pickle cucumbers in the front yard. When I lived in China, every meal started with pao tsai, pickled vegetables. Then I moved to Germany and stumbled upon entire festivals devoted to the pickle. So I've been to places where people rave about pickles, but I've never been to a pickle rave. But we caught up with someone who has.

DAN PANCOAST: They had handed out, like, glow bracelets and glow necklaces, and everyone was just dancing and having a good time.

SCHMITZ: That is Dan Pancoast. Recently, he went to The Big Dill Pickle Festival, where they had a pickle rave. And...

PANCOAST: They have a brine chug. They give you a solo cup full of pickle brine. That was, like, the first thing that I put in my stomach today.

SCHMITZ: Pancoast is a content creator who lives in Pennsylvania, and he loves pickles.

PANCOAST: My tattoo is basically a dill pickle with a sombrero on, wearing sunglasses.

UNIDENTIFIED ANNOUNCER: It is National Pickle Day in Philadelphia, everybody.

(CHEERING)

PANCOAST: I walked up to the venue, and there was a good bit of people outside...

UNIDENTIFIED ANNOUNCER: Who's ready for the parade of pickles?

PANCOAST: ...Probably a couple hundred people wearing pickle hats, pickle shirts, sweatshirts, costumes.

UNIDENTIFIED ANNOUNCER: So the Grand Gherkin is here to help lead us.

PANCOAST: Now they're doing the world record parade. People dressed as pickles (laughter). It's quite amazing, honestly.

UNIDENTIFIED ANNOUNCER: To clear the space for the count.

SCHMITZ: Pancoast said the festival exceeded his expectations. It was a sort of picklepalooza (ph).

PANCOAST: And no matter what kind of pickles you love, what style, what you like your pickles on, don't like your pickles on, how you eat them, everyone can just be here. There's no real - anything else to think about. You can't really overthink it (laughter).

SCHMITZ: That was Dan Pancoast. The Big Dill Festival did, in fact, break the record for people dressed like pickles - 1,597 pickled people.

(SOUNDBITE OF KAYTRANADA SONG, "WEIRD")

entries.title: Lebanese villagers return to wrecked homes as the Israeli army pulls back
entries.summary: In a pilot project in a village in southern Lebanon, Israeli forces have left and the Lebanese army moved it. But villagers who return find their houses wrecked.
entries.content:
ZAWTAR AL-GHARBIYAH, Lebanon — After two decades of working installing vehicle air conditioning in Saudi Arabia, Atef Kadouh saved up enough money to build a house in his hometown in southern Lebanon.

He and his wife, Soumaya Yaghi lived in the house for 40 years and had five children — all born at home.

Now there are four.

A photo of the youngest, Adel, is propped up in a basket of dried flowers near the doorway.

Adel, clean-cut with a trimmed beard, was a sports teacher and a basketball champion who was planning to travel to France this summer to pursue his doctorate. When the war with Israel began this year, he decided to volunteer as an ambulance driver.

The Israeli military killed him and four other medics on March 28 in a drone strike as the first responders buried a 75-year-old man who had died in hospital.

"This one broke me," his father says. "He was my youngest son, 27 years old. There have been wars in every country in the world but there are rules for war … you attack a paramedic rescuing wounded people, children? He was not a fighter at the front."

He says he warned his son that Israel could not be trusted not to kill medical personnel.

"He would not listen to me. He said, 'Dad there are wounded children — we have to go rescue them,'" he says.

Lebanon's Health Ministry says Israel has killed more than 135 first responders and medical staff in the past two years.

Asked about this airstrike, the Israeli military replied, without providing proof, that militants routinely pose as paramedics and transport weapons in ambulances for the militant group Hezbollah and its allies.

It did not respond to follow-up questions pointing out the five were not killed in an ambulance but at a burial.

A test case

The Kadouh family returned to the village in July when it became the first and until now only test of a U.S.-brokered plan for Israeli forces to withdraw and the Lebanese army to take over.

The plan is aimed at keeping Iran-backed Hezbollah out of the area, after they started firing rockets across the nearby border in solidarity with the Palestinian militant group Hamas who launched a surprise attack on southern Israel in October 2023.

Israel responded with devastating air strikes and eventually a ground invasion, and says it has continued attacks in south Lebanon following a U.S.-brokered ceasefire this year to eliminate what it believes are continued threats to northern Israel. Israel's defense minister has acknowledged destroying more than 20,000 homes across the Lebanese border in a self-declared security zone.

When Kadouh and Yaghi returned to the village, they found that Israeli soldiers had occupied their house. And then it had been set on fire.

Wrecked home

Upstairs in the hallway, near scorched walls and shattered windows, what appeared to be a work roster was written on the wall in blue marker in Hebrew with the first names of Israeli soldiers.

Almost everything in the house had been destroyed. Appliances — the fridge, freezer and washing machine — had bullet holes in them. Some, along with furniture, had been pushed over the second floor balcony, smashing on the ground below.

Kadouh says they knew from satellite photos there was destruction in their village "but the level of destruction — we were not expecting that. Everything that could be broken they broke."

In the kitchen were shattered floor tiles and kitchen cupboards wrenched from the walls.

The fire appeared to be set as the soldiers were leaving. Blackened, burned food packets — fruit boxes and cans of energy drinks with Hebrew writing — were on the floor along with rotting sandwiches.

In their 18-month-old grandson's bedroom, soot from a scorched ceiling dripped down on walls decorated with images of hot-air balloons and teddy bears climbing ladders to the moon.

Yaghi shows a bullet — one of many she says she found throughout the house. The spent engine casing of a missile or a drone with English markings reading "propulsion unit – tactical" was found in one of the rooms.

There is no running water or electricity — Kadouh says the Israeli military destroyed the solar panels.

The Lebanese army told them that when it reentered the village many of the houses had been rigged to be blown up. It said it dismantled explosives left by Israeli forces in their house and others.

The Israeli army did not reply to NPR queries about why the house was damaged or set on fire. It said military policy bars burning homes or leaving explosives.

Unable to enter the village while Israeli forces were there, Kadouh said he saw a tank in their courtyard from drone images posted on social media.

Even the trees destroyed

Yaghi says the Israeli army used a bulldozer to uproot the trees — including the pine trees which yield one of their most prized cash crops: pine nuts. When they had killed the trees, she says they demolished the family's garage and destroyed their tractor.

"We are back to square one," Kadouh says. "Starting from scratch."

Even more precarious, though, than when they started decades ago. Despite a ceasefire, smoke rises from a nearby village where Israel is still attacking.

Amid all the damage, the destruction of the family's trees cuts the deepest.

"I tended to them as if they were small children — they were all dear to me," Kadouh says.

Yaghi points out where there were fruit-bearing cactus, olive trees, a fig tree one of her sons brought from Italy, avocado trees and fields of thyme, avocado.

Up until a decade ago, almost everyone here grew tobacco, diversifying crops when that market collapsed.

"We raised our children through hard work and thank God all of them were educated," Yaghi says, noting with pride that they all became professionals.

She maintains a visceral connection to the land.

"Record this," she asks, walking next to rose bushes that have begun to bloom again. "Our land is a paradise with everything in it. Our life is this land. Our life is our homes. Even if we were to die in our homes it would be much better than to live outside."

Villagers here feel abandoned by even their own government — and still in danger from nearby Israeli forces.

"Our homes were destroyed and no one came to check on us," Kadouh says. "Not the Lebanese state or outsiders or the parties," he says, referring to Hezbollah and its allies. "They just say 'Go back, go back' to the village. We came back and there are no essentials — no electricity, no water."

Kadouh has a son in the Lebanese army and another in national security services but he says, because the Lebanese army is deliberately underequipped to avoid presenting a threat to Israel, they have never been allowed to do their jobs.

"The Lebanese state never sent a soldier here to protect us," he says." That is why the parties and others came in — Hezbollah or Amal or even the Palestinian factions decades ago. "But the vacuum that the Lebanese state has left brought us to this tragedy" he says.

"We love the Lebanese army — let them bring us an army, but let them protect us," he says. "This army has a rifle — Israel has an F-35" fighter jet.

"But we would rather sit in the dirt," he says. "Our soul, our life is here, I was born here."

Kadouh says maybe someday there will be peace with Israel, but after all the deaths and destruction, not in his lifetime — and not with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"Netanyahu is the one who killed my son. Let him bring back my son," he says. "If just yesterday Israel killed my son, am I supposed to tell the Israelis, 'Put your hand in my hand'? If they want to be our neighbors they should do good. Instead they burn us."

entries.title: Meet the young authors! A literacy program inspires kids in South Africa
entries.summary: South Africa is working to overcome a children's literacy crisis. In one Johannesburg township, a reading club is instilling a love of books in kids — and inspiring them to become authors.
entries.content:
JOHANNESBURG — It's an ordinary Saturday morning in Alexandra township, known simply as Alex or sometimes dubbed Gomora, a reference to the biblical city of Gomorrah that was known for its wickedness.

That nickname stems from Alexandra's high crime rates. It's a high-density area, where modest brick houses and tin shacks stretch as far as the eye can see and rotting garbage piles up along potholed streets.

But that image doesn't intrude on an event at a small building at the Kwabhekilanga Sports Ground. There's a palpable sense of excitement. Something different is happening this weekend and community members have turned up for it.

It's a book launch for a collection entitled From Gomora to the World. Stories from Alex. The seven stories in the self-published anthology have been written by children from the township who attend a free weekly literacy program.

South Africa is in the midst of a literacy crisis, with one international study showing a majority of 10-year-olds — some 81% — are unable to read for meaning in any of South Africa's 12 official languages.

The grassroots program Read Alex has been trying to change this, offering a weekend reading club, mainly in English, to instill a love of books in children. Launched by the Run Alex Athletics Club, it has about 50 participants. Among the activities: an annual public speaking competition, two spelling bees and a book drive on Mandela Day every year that brings in about 500 volumes — some of which the kids take home and some of which go to libraries.

Now, not only are the children getting to practice their reading, some of them have tried their hand at writing their own stories.

The newly published authors sit up front, ready to sign the pile of freshly-printed books for sale and answer questions about their process.

Thirteen-year-old Fiona Mogane, the bespectacled author of "Lindani's Modelling Journey," is one of them.

"It's about a girl who discovered a lot of challenges throughout her journey," Fiona explains. One of those challenges is that the main character Lindani's mother is an alcoholic, spending what little money the family has on drink — including government grant money meant for her daughter's welfare. She also shouts at her daughter a lot, and sometimes Lindani worries she will follow in her mother's footsteps.

Fiona writes: "Sometimes a thought intrudes on Lindani's mind, telling her that if she took some alcohol, it would make her feel better and stand up for herself …. However Lindani always pulls herself out of that thought: she knows she is stronger than that."

Phelelisa Somana, one of the coordinators of the book project, says she was impressed with the maturity of Fiona's story.

"When I read her story it had a very deep theme that I didn't expect a child to delve into in a way that she did," says Somana.

It "definitely just reminded me just how much kids are a lot smarter than they think they are," she adds. "They notice a lot more than they think they do."

Learning "Ubuntu"

Fortunately, Fiona's tale has a happy ending. Dreaming of becoming the next Miss South Africa, her character Lindani decides to try and raise the money she needs to enter a modelling contest by baking scones and selling them to her neighbors.

"She believes deep down inside that each one of her homemade scones has something special that makes them really delicious," Fiona writes.

In the end, Lindani makes enough cash to enter the contest. She comes in second place and is crowned "princess."

"She is happy because she has proved to herself that she can make a way when it initially seemed there was none," Fiona writes.

In real life, Fiona — also keen on modeling — is being raised in Alex by a single mom. Alex has high crime rates and poor government services like water and electricity. The young teenager is all too familiar with the problems, but she says there are good things about township life too..

"Alex is a crowded place, but when you're in Alex, you can learn a lot of things," she explains. "You can learn how to have Ubuntu."

Ubuntu is an African philosophy centering on community well-being and shared responsibility. As Fiona puts it: "Ubuntu is to help other people when they are in need."

Fiona, whose favorite subject at school is English, says she'd like to go to university, maybe to study medicine. And there's another dream too.

"One day, if I grow up, I want to build a big house that will be having a room with its own books," she says.

Homes without books

Fiona didn't grow up with books at home. Two-thirds of South African children don't have books at home, according to one study by UNICEF. 

They won't necessarily find them at school either.

Only about 15% of public schools in South Africa have a functioning library, according to government data.

The dire state of child literacy has its roots in the home. Many children have weak early learning foundations, according to the UNICEF study, and they have no exposure to books before starting primary school.

"When I became the minister of basic education in 2024 I was confronted by the statistic of 80% of 10-year-olds who cannot read for meaning in any language," Basic Education Minister Siviwe Gwarube told NPR.

The minister says the government is trying to tackle this problem by getting more kids into early learning programs.

"We're investing ten billion rand [$58 million] over the next three years on a massive haul out of early childhood development centers," Gwarube says.

Tebogo Selekane, an English teacher at Kwa-bhekilanga secondary school, says the weekend program at Read Alex has helped some of her students a lot. Two of her students have stories in the book.

"They are doing very well in reading," says Selekane. "There's a lot of change in them... they will respond back with confidence."

A country of storytellers

At the book launch, Wandile Mathe, a 21-year-old South African writer and joint coordinator of the project, says despite South Africa's poor literacy rates, the children he coaches come from a nation of storytellers.

"I think South Africans are natural storytellers," he says. "There's always gossip going around anyway."

"In the taxi, at the line, in a shop, wherever you go, there's always someone willing to tell you a story, whether about their personal life or the things that they're seeing around," he laughs. "We're huge social commentators. Nothing will pass by and we will not comment."

The kids who contributed to the book are true to this storytelling tradition, borrowing from their lives and what they see daily in the township. As well as Fiona's story about poverty and alcoholism, there are tales about peer pressure, dangerous men on the street, losing parents and inability to pay school fees.

But it's not all doom and gloom. The heroes and heroines all find ways to overcome the obstacles, learning important lessons and making friends along the way.

For example, one of the young authors, 13-year-old Anita Maloka, wrote a story about a rural girl who moves to Johannesburg to attend school and dreams of becoming a scientist. But the school is not what she hoped.

"Sometimes two students had to squeeze together on one chair. Textbooks were scarce," she writes. The family doesn't have the money to send her anywhere better though, so the character works toward earning a scholarship at a school that "has a real science lab and an entire room just for learning to program computers and building robots."

Like her character, Anita, who dreams of becoming a marine biologist, is also working toward getting a scholarship that will take her out of the township.

But she stresses that life in Alex is "not just about struggle."

"It's about children who want to travel, to explore and dream and make their dreams come true," she says.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

entries.title: Climate change talks fall apart in final hours over fossil fuels
entries.summary: Some 200 countries gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the annual climate negotiations. Countries failed to reach an agreement over fossil fuels - the primary driver of global warming.
entries.content:
Climate change talks fall apart in final hours over fossil fuels

ANTALYA, Turkey – International climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours with a disagreement over how to address fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

On Sunday, delegates from nearly 200 countries failed to reach an overall agreement covering targets for electrification, finance to help developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change, and how to respond to the fact that the planet will soon breach a key warming threshold.

The talks ran two days longer than expected, becoming the longest climate conference in the history of these summits. And it ended in a dramatic fashion, with delegates from the European Union rejecting any final outcome that did not explicitly call for a transition away from fossil fuels. Some oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia opposed such language. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal makes up roughly 73% of global emissions.

Ireland's Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Darragh O'Brien, who spoke for the EU, soon left the room, along with EU Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth Wopke Hoekstra.

Other countries also objected to the text, including Panama, Belize, and small island states such as Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands.

Hoekstra said that with the world heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."

This is the first U.N. climate summit where there's been formal acknowledgment that the world will surpass a key global warming threshold. Countries agreed in 2015 to try to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.

Passing that threshold means more severe climate impacts, like more intense hurricanes and heat waves. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius would require cutting emissions immediately, reducing them by 45% by 2035. That, scientists say, would require dramatically cutting fossil fuel use.

Meanwhile, the transition away from fossil fuels is happening regardless of what the U.N. agreements say, says Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who ran the negotiations.

"The transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is inevitable," Bowen told the press after the agreement failed. "It's happening at speed and it's irreversible."

Disagreements on fossil fuels

The disagreements over mentioning fossil fuels in climate conferences have a long, fractured history.

The COP process works by consensus, so nearly 200 countries must agree to a final text at the end of the negotiations. Some fossil fuel producers like Norway and Mexico have recently wanted to include transitioning away from fossil fuels in the text. Other large oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia and Russia have blocked adding fossil fuels to the final agreement.

At the climate talks in Dubai in 2023, countries agreed for the first time in 28 years of conferences to mention transitioning away from fossil fuels in the final agreement.

Deeply frustrated with this U.N. process, more than 50 countries have created their own separate conference dedicated to phasing out fossil fuels. In April, they held the "First International Conference for the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels" in Colombia. In 2027, Ireland and the Pacific Island nation of Tuvalu will co-host the second conference.

These side efforts are the best hope for climate action until something changes in the COP process, says Juan Carlos Navarro, environment minister of Panama.

"I am an optimist by nature," he tells NPR, "but I am not an idiot."

Increasing electrification

This year, the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and the unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz loomed over the negotiations.

Since the war began, countries across Asia and Africa have accelerated their transitions to solar energy, batteries and electric vehicles, and reduced their reliance on fossil fuels like oil and natural gas.

COP31 organizers promised that this would be the "electrification COP." Climate technologies like renewable energy, super-efficient heat pumps and electric vehicles are also called electrification technologies. Many of these technologies are being manufactured in China, the main exporter of climate solutions.

The conference's initial goal was to increase global electrification from its current level of around 23% to 35% by 2035. "So 35 by '35 is the mantra," Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember, told NPR when COP31 began.

The 35 by 35 electrification pledge was signed on to by dozens of countries. However, that pledge did not ultimately pass, says Alden Meyer, a senior associate at the climate change think tank E3G. "Electrification was collateral damage when the whole decision cratered," he said.

Lack of U.S. Presence

The Trump administration did not send a delegation to COP31 for a second year in a row. President Trump announced he would withdraw the U.S. from the Paris Agreement on his first day back in office in 2025. Trump has called climate change a hoax, and his administration has rolled back regulations on climate pollution and funding for wind and solar power and electric vehicles.

An informal delegation of congressional Democrats did come to Turkey. They told delegates at COP31 that when Democrats control both chambers of Congress next year, climate change will return to the main agenda.

Billions of dollars still needed

While the debate over fossil fuels stole the spotlight at this year's COP, a major focus of the negotiations has been on money. Countries debated new goals for funding to assist nations hardest hit by climate change.

Over the years at climate summits, lower-income countries have made the case that while they're responsible for only a small share of the emissions causing climate change, they're experiencing some of the worst disasters.

"We're not a nation that has the luxury of debating whether climate change is real for us," says Matthew Samuda, Jamaica's minister of water, environment and climate change. "The reality is, over the last five years, we have had a category 4 hurricane, a tropical storm and a category 5 hurricane. So climate change for us is indeed real and we are experiencing economic losses from a problem that we didn't create."

In 2024, nations agreed to eventually provide $1.3 trillion per year to developing nations, what's known as climate finance. Only about $136.7 billion was delivered in 2024, according to a report from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. The majority of that goes to projects that reduce emissions, including renewable energy like solar and wind.

As climate disasters become costlier, lower-income countries have been pushing for more funding to adapt to climate impacts, such as protecting coastal communities from sea level rise and strengthening infrastructure against storms. The United Nations estimates that those nations' needs will reach $305 billion annually by 2035.

During the talks in Turkey, developing nations pushed for more concrete commitments to deliver adaptation funding. But those elements to deliver on tripling adaptation funding by 2035 were in the larger decision that was ultimately rejected, Meyer says.

"Vulnerable countries from Africa and elsewhere are quite angry about that outcome," he says.

Earlier this year, countries requested $2.8 billion to help with damages, but only $342 million in funding was available.

At the COP31 summit, only $142 million in additional funding was pledged, far less than in other recent COP summits.

NPR correspondent Michael Copley contributed to this story. This story was edited by Sadie Babits.

Correction Nov. 22, 2026

A previous version of this story incorrectly said the European Union walked out along with other countries. In fact, EU representatives walked out while other countries objected.

entries.title: Medicare looks a bit different in 2027, so don't miss open enrollment
entries.summary: Open enrollment for Medicare runs through Dec. 7, and there are a few different pitfalls people should watch out for this year. Your drug plan or Medicare Advantage plan could be changing a lot.
entries.content:
Medicare looks a bit different in 2027, so don't miss open enrollment

Annual open enrollment is underway for Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance to roughly 70 million people. The coverage choices are complex and often consequential.

Open enrollment runs through Dec. 7. The plan you choose takes effect on Jan. 1, for the full calendar year.

Build-your-own Medicare menu

Medicare provides health insurance to people 65 or older, as well as to some younger people with disabilities or certain health conditions. But it isn't one plan. It's more like a build-your-own-insurance menu.

Roughly half of beneficiaries are enrolled in traditional Medicare, which consists of Parts A and B. Administered by the federal government, the plan covers hospital stays, skilled nursing care, doctor visits, outpatient care, and preventive screenings. Enrollees can typically see any healthcare provider who accepts Medicare, and they rarely need approval for diagnostic tests, such as MRIs and CT scans. However, there's no cap on out-of-pocket expenses in traditional Medicare, and it doesn't cover most prescriptions or dental, vision, or hearing services.

As a result, most traditional Medicare enrollees buy extra coverage from private insurance companies under Medicare Part D, the prescription drug plan. Some also buy a Medigap policy that covers the costs traditional Medicare leaves behind, such as deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance.

Medicare Advantage

This year, the other half of Medicare beneficiaries opted for privately offered, all-in-one managed-care plans known as Medicare Advantage, usually including prescription drug coverage, dental, and vision. The drawbacks are smaller networks and a greater likelihood that treatments and medications will require prior authorization. Like beneficiaries in traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage participants also pay Part B premiums.

"People really need to do their research before they enroll in Medicare, because there are trade-offs," said David Lipschutz, a co-director at the Center for Medicare Advocacy.

The hassle saves money

Every fall, insurers that offer Part D and Advantage plans send enrollees a critical document known as an Annual Notice of Change. It's a cheat sheet outlining what will be different in the following year: premiums, deductibles, covered drugs. Consumer advocates and Medicare experts say people sometimes make the costly mistake of throwing it out or filing it away without reading it. Can't find it? Call the insurer and ask for another copy.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services projects that the average Part D premium will increase less than $1 a month for a standalone prescription drug plan, describing the market as stable. But that average doesn't tell the whole story. An analysis by KFF, the health policy research nonprofit that includes KFF Health News, found that enrollees who stay in their prescription drug plan will see a 50% increase on average, from $34 to $51. About 10.4 million people could pay higher premiums, not including higher deductibles and coinsurance costs.

Some beneficiaries who didn't have to pay monthly premiums in recent years will begin paying for prescription drug Part D coverage in 2027. While that change follows the 2025 introduction of federal caps on out-of-pocket drug expenses, it comes as the Trump administration is ending temporary federal subsidies that helped keep premiums down. The cap on out-of-pocket expenses for prescription drugs in 2027 will be $2,400, a total enrollees can opt tospread out over the course of the year.

Juliette Cubanski, who directs the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, said people who don't shop around could be leaving money on the table.

"It is worth it to avoid any unpleasant surprises in the form of either higher premiums or higher cost sharing for covered services in 2027," she said.

Some plans no longer offered

An estimated 4.3 million people now have to look for a new Medicare Advantage or prescription drug plan after private insurers left the market. Those who want to stay in Medicare Advantage must select new coverage, or they'll be moved to traditional Medicare automatically. For those shopping for a new plan, low monthly premiums may be appealing, but it's important to read the fine print and add up the other costs.

"There are going to be, often, increases in cost sharing and copays, increases in out-of-pocket caps, and reductions in the scope of some of the extra benefits that Medicare Advantage plans provide," Lipschutz said.

So ask: Is my prescription covered? Is my pharmacy preferred? Is my doctor in-network? What does the dental benefit actually cover?

And pay attention to the out-of-pocket maximum for the Advantage plans, Cubanski said, so you know how much you might have to shell out in 2027.

"Look at that dollar value specifically," she said.

For those moving to traditional Medicare, it won't come with a drug plan, so enrollees must sign up for a new Part D plan if they want most prescriptions covered. Enrollees who miss that step when they are first eligible may not have drug coverage for the coming year, and they may face a late-enrollment penalty on their monthly premiums for life.

When selecting a drug plan, enrollees must also tell their insurer how they want to pay, either by getting a bill in the mail or by having the cost deducted from their Social Security. If you don't pick a payment plan, you could get dropped from coverage.

If enrollees elect to leave their Medicare Advantage plans for traditional Medicare within their first year of joining Medicare, they have a guaranteed right to buy a Medigap plan, with no health screening. After that, all bets are off: Insurers in most states can turn enrollees down or charge more because of a health condition. Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, and New York are exceptions.

Enrollees whose Advantage plans have not been renewed — and haven't been consolidated into another plan — can switch to traditional Medicare and buy a Medigap policy without a health screening, but they need to act before March.

For shopping help, think "SHIP"

Medicare experts advise enrollees to write down all their prescription drugs, as well as any procedures planned in the next year, such as a joint replacement or dental work, to help them decide which plan will cover their needs. Call a favorite doctor's office to see whether they are in-network for the plans being considered. Remember that brokers might earn commissions, especially on Advantage plans, and might not represent every plan.

For unbiased help, every state has a federally funded State Health Insurance Assistance Program that offers free plan counseling specific to your situation, in person and over the phone. To get help, go to the website at shiphelp.org/open-enrollment, email info@shiphelp.org, or call the SHIP National Technical Assistance Center at 877-839-2675.

A SHIP counselor can also help enrollees apply for benefits that help pay for Medicare premiums and prescription drug costs, such as the Medicare Savings Programs and Medicare Part D Extra Help.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

entries.title: He expected a small-business loan. He got a 7-year nightmare
entries.summary: America's fastest-growing source of funding for small businesses is also one of the least regulated. One man has waged a long, lonely fight to recoup its punishing cost.
entries.content:
GLENDALE, Calif. — Sitting at his desk, tucked into a corner of his teenage bedroom — a place where he'd never intended to return, well into middle age — Vahe Shahinian rereads the emails that split his life into before and after.

A broker was offering to fund Shahinian's small business with a line of credit worth $750,000.

It was 2019, and Shahinian's company soared, like a miniature Live Nation-Ticketmaster, selling tickets and producing concerts around Los Angeles and beyond. He imagined how much he could do with stable funding.

The pitch had a catch: Shahinian would first accept a third of the sum and start paying it back immediately, in daily installments of $3,600. After 30 days, he could access the rest of the money. He crunched the numbers, followed up with questions — and took the deal.

Shahinian sent the daily payments, he says, for 30 days. Then 40. Then 50.

The line of credit never came.

"From that day," he says, "it's been one long day, one long nightmare."

For seven years, Shahinian has been mired in the shadowy industry that is now the fastest-growing source of funding for small business in the United States. It's largely unregulated, promising fast money at a tremendous cost. And Shahinian's lawsuit against his funders could become one of the first of its kind to go to trial.

A business in need

Before the "incident," as Shahinian calls his fateful deal, he'd been in business for 15 years, building his company from a side hustle into his main source of income.

Educated as a computer scientist, he'd spent years programming satellites as an aerospace engineer. In 2004, he also developed a site for something he loved in his spare time: community events. Shahinian called his platform for ticketing and seating charts It's My Seat.

Over a decade, Shahinian grew his business from selling tickets to galas and festivals to producing his own shows: booking artists and venues, promoting and marketing. His first concert, by a flamenco guitarist, sold 400 seats. The next, 700. Three years later, 1960s crooner Engelbert Humperdinck performed for 3,000. In 2015, Shahinian expanded again, into touring.

Like most U.S. small businesses, Shahinian says, he self-funded for years. Entrepreneurs like him often dip into savings, family money or home equity; many run up credit cards and reinvest profits.

Shahinian says he had qualified for several generous credit cards, including an American Express with essentially no spending limit. Later, Amex also repeatedly approved him for special merchant financing: instant short-term loans with a low interest rate of 6%.

"All my life," Shahinian offers as his frequent disclaimer these days, "I had never had one missed payment."

By 2018, Shahinian says, he had built his retirement plan: His ticket sales climbed toward $5 million a year, his profits $250,000.

Booking his biggest tour yet, with a 1980s German superstar, Shahinian sought his fifth round of Amex merchant funding.

Except this time, Amex said no. The company was phasing out the program.

All Shahinian could think was: "Whoa." Tours are costly affairs with down payments to venues, marketing, airfare, lights and sound. He'd left himself no time to maneuver — two weeks to acquire about $200,000.

Enter merchant cash advances.

A funding void

Small businesses in the U.S. consistently say they turn to merchant cash advances, MCAs, because they find few alternatives, especially in an emergency.

Most traditional lending takes months and vigorous vetting. The Small Business Administration has tightened its lending rules. Big banks reject about 20% of business loan applications, according to the Treasury Department, and respond to a quarter with only partial funding. A recent Federal Reserve survey found even lower odds.

MCAs, by contrast, present themselves as a lifeline, offering large sums within hours.

Their fees, however, run from 25% to 200% and more, when translated into an annual rate. MCA firms argue they charge a lot because they take on big risks.

They also face almost no regulatory oversight.

MCAs escape most lending laws because, technically, they are not loans. An MCA is meant to be a purchase of future sales — a business gets cash in exchange for a steady cut of its earnings later. MCA funders generally aren't required to be licensed and face no legal limit to how much they can charge.

The industry runs the gamut: A funder could be a firm recommended by Amazon, or the latest fintech startup, or a former subprime mortgage lender. Some rely on brokers to drum up deals. Most collect payment by withdrawing directly from their borrowers' bank accounts — often daily.

Shahinian, scrambling after the Amex rejection, lined up two cash advances for a total of $250,000, he says, owing back almost $400,000. This saved his concert tour but cost him all the profits.

"It was my fault — I waited last minute," Shahinian says. "I'm talking to myself, 'Vahe, you had to do it this time. You're never going back to MCAs.'"

A fateful offer

But MCA pitches never stop. Sometimes, Shahinian replied that he wanted only a traditional loan, something along an 8% interest rate.

Before he even went hunting, the offer came to him — the pitch that changed his life: The line of credit up to $750,000 at an annual interest rate just under 9%. Finally, Shahinian thought, someone recognized the quality of his business.

"It's like the puzzle fit, you know?" he says.

This encounter took Shahinian beyond the MCAs' unforgiving fees into what he alleges was fraud.

As he weighed the offer's condition — 30 days of daily $3,600 payments — he didn't recognize it as a merchant cash advance.

On the phone, the broker presented it as a routine test, Shahinian says, to show his dependability before he'd qualify for his preapproved line of credit. Shahinian had no lawyer or adviser to consult then. He looked up the finance firm, Wall Street-based EIN Cap; it advertised itself as a "provider of working capital to local businesses."

"I was assured that 'We've done this for years. We don't care about a 30-day program — our goal is long term,'" Shahinian says. "The whole setup was to make someone like me feel assured, feel safe — and I felt safe to go in it."

From the start, Shahinian says, he received $228,000 instead of the promised $250,000. The difference was withheld as an initial fee, a common feature of MCAs. He set aside almost half the funds to secure his daily $3,600 payment. The rest vanished into down payments for venues and other tour investments.

After 30 days, when the line of credit didn't materialize, Shahinian says the broker portrayed the delays as technical. His emails grew urgent.

"I had calculated and planned everything based on the 30-day plan."

"I planned massive tour projects based on this solid word. This is not a joke."

"I don't think you understand the urgency of this situation. I'm basically out of time."

EIN Cap later in court argued it never promised Shahinian any loans or lines of credit — only a merchant cash advance, which it delivered. EIN Cap said it was the brokers — the middlemen — who had arranged the deal and made promises. Much of what the company had to say about its ties to those brokers is in sealed depositions.

After 40 days of daily payments, Shahinian says, for the first time, his bank account hit zero.

A spiral of debt

Shahinian's lawyer, Shane Heskin — who has been clashing with MCA companies for a decade — calls what happened here "carroting." As in, a carrot gets dangled in front of a small-business owner in the form of an attractive financing deal — a low-interest loan — in a bait and switch to sign an unsolicited MCA.

"I see two or three a week," Heskin says about such cases. "They're exploding."

Heskin says common targets are first-time business owners, first-time borrowers and especially immigrants.

NPR spoke with several entrepreneurs who were "carroted" in similar ways. One described falling into a deep depression; another declared bankruptcy. None, except Shahinian, wanted to speak on the record.

Shahinian says he paid his unwanted MCA to the end, hemorrhaging cash.

"That's just who I am, you know?" he says, explaining his choice. "Who I was."

In fact, had he stopped paying, his funders might have sued him for debt collection — a common consequence with MCAs.

Days before his biggest concert tour yet, with his accounts empty, Shahinian assessed costs: venues still half-paid, airfare unbooked and rising in price, thousands of tickets undermarketed and unsold.

He did what many business owners do when they struggle to stay afloat with merchant cash advances: He took out more cash advances.

A collapse

Shahinian says his two new MCAs, totaling around $250,000, evaporated into expenses in half a day.

"From here," he says, "the avalanche of money over money, over money, over money started."

He tapped his credit and then home equity — his own, his parents' and his best friend's. Within weeks, Shahinian says, he was more than $1 million in debt to friends and family.

"He asked me for some money, and, I mean, I could see he's drowning, you know?" says Zorik Yeghikian, who did lend to Shahinian later on. He's a restaurant owner whom Shahinian had helped win a catering contract for a local concert venue.

Yeghikian knew the trap of MCA payments. They had nearly capsized his own business, he says, when he'd borrowed about $30,000 and owed nearly triple. Yeghikian slept at his restaurant and worked double shifts alongside his wife, both forgoing pay.

"I lost my hair," Yeghikian says. "I went through hell those years."

The exact scale of the MCA industry is unclear, but it's ballooning. The Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City reports that businesses are increasingly turning to MCAs to cover basic expenses like payroll. MCAs are a frequent feature in small-business bankruptcies, which have been rising.

Shahinian canceled several concerts of his tours, costing him six-figure losses. Many shows went underpromoted and undersold. They might have seemed OK to the audience but did little to save him.

He began to default on his debts.

Shahinian watched himself become someone who lost count of overdue bills and unpaid invoices. He tapped more emergency MCAs and raked in collections notices. Some of his clients received lien letters, asking them to redirect any payments meant for Shahinian to his funders instead. His business relationships wore thin. His social circle shrunk.

He huddled in his home office with his tuxedo cats, Koby and Toby, and faced the existential dilemma: fight or flight?

A fight or a fold

Shahinian's choice — to fight — is rare. Borrowers often struggle to afford lawyers, let alone find one familiar with the MCA industry.

And MCA firms can be difficult to pin down. Shahinian says he had to hire a private investigator to reach his funders to serve his lawsuit.

He sued EIN Cap and the brokers in 2019. Three years later, he settled his claims against the brokers to focus on EIN. His remaining case in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles accuses EIN of fraud.

"EIN Cap denies Mr. Shahinian's claims, and its position is set out in its public court filings," Levi Silver, counsel for EIN, said in an emailed statement, declining any further comment due to the pending case.

As Shahinian's lawsuit plodded through the legal system, he descended down its rabbit hole.

"Most people settle, but no one depended on this promise like I did, to this magnitude," Shahinian says. "There's no way I was gonna go down. I decided to fight it to the end."

He scoured the web for people associated with his lending deal.

He found his broker, who'd introduced himself as Bryan Stein, used different names and been indicted for financial crimes. The Brooklyn District Attorney's Office told NPR that the man, Boris Shteyngart, pleaded guilty in 2012 to grand larceny; public records show he served time in prison.

Shahinian spent a year tracking down some 700 business owners who'd been sued by EIN for debt collection.

Most did not want to revisit that chapter. Shahinian says that he connected with 70 and that many "came to tears" because "someone is standing up to bullies."

In the past decade, EIN has faced several lawsuits in at least nine states, records show. Most cases related to bankruptcies by its MCA borrowers, and most were settled or dismissed. In one case in Washington state, EIN was ordered to return the daily fees it continued to withdraw from a business that was already insolvent.

Last year, a U.S. district judge in Illinois ruled against EIN in a case over its 2019 MCA funding to a firm that federal regulators accuse of running a Ponzi-like scheme. The judge wrote that EIN "propped up" and "prolonged the Ponzi scheme" by either failing to conduct due diligence or ignoring its findings, and must return profits of $184,854.

Meanwhile in California, Shahinian's trial was delayed by another nine months. Shortly after, he lost his house to a foreclosure.

A suspended reality

For 16 years, Shahinian lived in a lush suburban cul-de-sac in the vibrant Armenian American community of Glendale, north of downtown Los Angeles. In front of his former house is an ancient oak tree; the backyard spills onto the foot of a mountain.

At age 51, Shahinian sold off belongings, packed up his cats, computer screens, ticket printers and prized sound system — and moved in with his elderly parents.

Every dollar from the foreclosure sale, Shahinian says, went to pay mortgage debt and part of the debt to his best friend.

Several friends have urged him to move on from his costly seven-year legal fight, perhaps declare bankruptcy. To him, that's admitting defeat.

"My fault," he says, "was only believing in a promise that I could have never imagined to be false."

In recent years, a handful of states, including California, have started requiring MCA companies to be clearer, in writing, about their fees. And California recently also passed a law that, starting in 2028, will require funders and brokers to be licensed and undergo background checks and inspections.

It's too late for Shahinian.

His business is now back to basics: ticketing, mostly for local shows, and coding bells and whistles for his marketing software. He hopes his lawsuit will recoup more than $5 million — all the debt Shahinian estimates he has accrued since his "incident," including some $3 million in interest and fees.

He lays blame for its entirety at the feet of his funders, with a car-accident comparison. "You're being rear-ended," he says. "The 12-wheeler rear-ending you, you lose the steering wheel, and you smash into a bunch of cars, and everyone's focus is: Why did you smash into a bunch of cars?"

Heskin, Shahinian's lawyer, says the best-case scenario would be a multimillion-dollar judgment with punitive damages, "and then it's good luck collecting on it."

He's not sure what assets EIN or its employees named in Shahinian's lawsuit still have. NPR asked EIN's lawyers whether the firm still operates; they didn't respond. The firm's investors are unknown.

Shahinian argues any win would be meaningful.

"It would show everyone [whom] I affected these years that I'm in the right," he says. "Hopefully it would be a case for the industry to self-heal, self-correct. Maybe. And it'll be hope for others who are stuck — give them motivation."

"Don't give up, you know?" he says. "Don't be on path of least resistance. Go fighting."

He chuckles and pumps his fist up in the air.

NPR's Will Chase contributed to this report.

entries.title: NPR's Senior Podcast Challenge: Early entries we love
entries.summary: People 65 and older have been submitting stories for a chance to win our grand prize — a visit to NPR watch your podcast air live on Weekend Edition. There's still time to enter!
entries.content:
Once people hit retirement age, there are so many questions: Who am I without my job? What do I do to fill this time? How are my relationships changing?

This fall, for the first-ever NPR Senior Podcast Challenge, we asked those of you in the over-65 crowd, to tell us about all this, and you've been sending in your answers.

The competition flips the story line on our popular NPR Student Podcast Challenge – since 2018 more than 90,000 young people have sent us their stories, in their own voices.

Now, we're hearing from listeners with a lot of experience, hopefully some wisdom, and perhaps more grey hair.

While the contest is still open for a few more weeks — you have until November 30 to enter — we've been listening to more than 100 podcasts that have come in so far.

Here's a sample of some of our early favorites:

Lou Ann Baylock, of Sarasota, Fla., told us she wasn't too happy about the title of our contest: the "senior" part.

"I'm 68, but I'm NOT a senior, am I?" she asks in her podcast, Talk to Me.

"I thought seniors were people in their 80s," she says. "I mean, I see my body changing. I know I'm getting older. But am I really a senior?"

Baylock ends up deciding she's OK with that term: She's still working, and as a therapist she tells us in her podcast she has some ideas that might help other people her age.

Finding the joy

Many of our podcasters took up the issue of life after retirement. Some of you are telling us you're having the best time of your life. Others, not so much.

For Martin Goldsmith, 78, of Tacoma, Wash., retirement means not letting his age keep him doing the things he loves.

"The back, the legs, and the joints aren't what they used to be," he says in his entry Joy Filled Retirement. "So for me, the running and skiing are out and the hearing aids are in."

But, he adds, "I can still play my guitar."

Music, Goldsmith tells us, has always been in his DNA. He grew up jamming with his dad on the clarinet and mom on the viola. And he's now playing his guitar at the children's hospital, and he ends his story playing and singing an old favorite, Nobody Knows You When You're Down and Out.

Putting yourself out there

And then, there's dating. We've received quite a few podcasts about life post-divorce, or after losing a partner.

Our podcasters are reminding us that it never gets easier, and many of them including George Smith have told us some version of this: "I never thought I'd be here."

Smith lives with his daughter in Wildomar, Calif., and when it came to figuring out the modern dating scene, he says:

"After almost three decades of marriage, I found myself in my mid-60s, divorced, alone in a cafe, and about to meet a woman from a dating app for the first time in my life. Little did I realize," he tells us, "my teenage daughter Shannon would become my dating navigator."

Smith's podcast is aptly called Swipe Right, Dad, and he tells us about three very different online dates he goes on.

Want to enter? Here are the details

Our competition, will close on Nov. 30. You can submit here.

Podcasts submitted must be completely original work, no longer than eight minutes in length. We encourage stories of all kinds – from personal narratives to in-depth interviews to fully reported audio journalism.

Some key rules: No copyrighted music. And, this should come as no surprise: keep AI out of your writing and presentation.

See the rules page for exact requirements and restrictions.

You can submit multiple podcasts. Please fill out a separate form for each entry.

We'll choose several finalists and our grand-prize winner early in the new year and air the winning podcast on Weekend Edition Sunday in January or February.

If you have no idea where to get started, don't worry! You don't need to be an audio expert, and you can make a podcast with nothing more than a smart phone, a computer, and some easily available editing software. You can check out our student podcasting resources page, which includes step-by-step instructions, from choosing a good story, conducting interviews, writing a script, and tips for editing and mixing. And you cansubscribe to our newsletter for the latest from the contest team.

And finally, if you have questions about the Senior Podcast Challenge, email us at seniorpodcastchallenge@npr.org.

entries.title: Trump orders federal contractors to check with White House before responding to Congress
entries.summary: President Trump is directing federal contractors to consult the White House about inquiries from Congress and to withhold any communications that his administration considers privileged.
entries.content:
Trump orders federal contractors to check with White House before responding to Congress

NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to a new executive order.

The companies must also coordinate with the White House and U.S. agencies on "appropriate responses" to any such requests, the order issued late Friday says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.

The order is the Republican administration's latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets, noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump's family, particularly at the Pentagon.

White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations initiated by Democrats.

Trump's counsel, Will Scharf, told federal agencies on Monday that they must seek approval from his office and the White House's Office of Legislative Affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to "blatant criminality."

Garcia sent letters this week directing members of Trump's family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance.

Responding to the new executive order, Garcia said it was part of the administration's "blatant attack on Congress' constitutional right to conduct oversight." He said that despite efforts to impede investigations, "we're just getting started."

In a fact sheet, the White House framed the new requirements as "protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach," arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by "harassing private companies that contract with the federal government."

Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute.

The latest executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, a universe of tens of thousands of businesses.
